title: Concurrency in Java: threads, locks and visibility
seriesDescription: Threads, synchronized, locks, volatile, executors, CompletableFuture, virtual threads, concurrent collections and classic drills. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Thread lifecycle and states, run versus start, synchronized versus ReentrantLock, volatile, happens-before, atomics, CAS, double-checked locking and interrupts.
source: Oracle Java docs (Thread, Object.wait, java.util.concurrent, ReentrantLock); JLS chapter 17 (memory model); Java Concurrency in Practice; Baeldung; GeeksforGeeks; DZone and InterviewBit multithreading lists

questions.prompt:
What does this Java snippet print?

```java
new Thread(() -> System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName()), "worker").run();
```

What is printed?

options.text: `main`, because `run()` executes on the calling thread
options.why: Correct: `run()` is an ordinary method call, so the lambda executes on the calling thread, which is `main`.

options.text: `worker`, the name given to the new thread
options.why: The name "`worker`" belongs to a thread that was never started; `run()` does not create one.

options.text: `Thread-0`, the default name of a new thread
options.why: `Thread-0` is the default name of the first thread created without a name, and no new thread starts here.

options.text: Nothing, because the thread is never started
options.why: `run()` executes the body synchronously, so it prints before the statement finishes.

questions.explanation: `start()` asks the JVM to create a new thread of execution that then calls `run()`. Calling `run()` directly is a plain method call. Interviewers love this trap.

questions.prompt: Match each `java.lang.Thread.State` with the situation that puts a thread in it.

right.text: Created with `new Thread(...)` but `start()` not yet called
Running on a CPU or ready to run
Trying to enter a `synchronized` block whose monitor another thread holds

questions.explanation: `Thread.State` has six values; the sixth (`TERMINATED`) is the distractor here. A thread contending for a monitor is `BLOCKED`, while one parked by `wait/join/LockSupport.park` is `WAITING`.

questions.prompt: Four threads each execute `count++` 250 times on a shared non-volatile `int` field that starts at 0, with no synchronization. What is the largest final value that is possible?
questions.explanation: Each increment adds at most 1, and there are 4 x 250 = 1000 increments, so 1000 is the upper bound. Lost updates only make the result smaller (and it can be much smaller). The interview point: `count++` is read, add, write, not atomic.

questions.prompt: Write a Java class `Counter` with a private `int` field, a method `increment()` and a method `int get()`, made thread-safe using the intrinsic lock (`synchronized`).
questions.explanation: Both methods must use the same lock: a synchronized reader gives visibility as well as mutual exclusion. `AtomicInteger` or `ReentrantLock` are other valid solutions; the grader accepts an explicit lock too.

questions.prompt: Given a field `ReentrantLock lock`, write a snippet that tries to acquire the lock for at most 1 second, runs `doWork()` only if it got the lock, and always releases it.

checks.label: uses TimeUnit or a time argument

questions.explanation: The unlock goes in `finally`, and the try starts only after the lock was acquired, otherwise you would unlock a lock you do not hold (`IllegalMonitorStateException`). `tryLock(timeout)` also throws `InterruptedException`.

questions.prompt: Select all features that `ReentrantLock` offers and the `synchronized` keyword does not.

options.text: A `tryLock()` that returns immediately or after a timeout
options.why: Correct: `synchronized` has no way to give up waiting for a monitor.

options.text: `lockInterruptibly()`, so a waiting thread can be interrupted
options.why: Correct: a thread blocked entering `synchronized` cannot be interrupted.

options.text: An optional fairness policy (`new ReentrantLock(true)`)
options.why: Correct: monitors give no fairness guarantee.

options.text: Automatic release if the guarded code throws an exception
options.why: False: this is a feature of `synchronized`; with `ReentrantLock` you must unlock in `finally`.

options.text: A thread may re-acquire a lock it already holds
options.why: True for both, so it does not distinguish the two.

questions.explanation: Choose `ReentrantLock` for `tryLock`, interruptible or timed waits, fairness and multiple Conditions. Otherwise `synchronized` is simpler and cannot leak a lock. Both are reentrant.

options.text: `inst is not volatile, so a thread may see a non-null reference to a partly constructed Cfg.`
options.why: Correct: without `volatile` the write of the reference can be reordered with the constructor's writes.

options.text: Two `Cfg` objects are always created, because the first null check is outside the `synchronized` block.
options.why: The second check inside `synchronized` prevents duplicates; the issue is safe publication.

options.text: It deadlocks because the `synchronized` block takes the lock on a Class object.
options.why: Locking `Cfg.class` is legal and cannot deadlock here.

options.text: Static fields cannot be read outside a `synchronized` block.
options.why: Static fields read fine; the problem is the missing happens-before edge.

questions.explanation: Fix with `private static volatile Cfg inst`, or use the initialization-on-demand holder idiom or an enum singleton. Since Java 5 `volatile` forbids that reordering.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.reason: A `volatile` write is visible to subsequent reads of that field by other threads.

whys.a: A is false, so this option cannot be right.
whys.b: A is false, so option b (both true) is wrong.
whys.c: A is false, so option c (A true) is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: volatile gives visibility and ordering, but counter++ is still read, add, write. Two threads can read the same value and both write back value + 1.

questions.explanation: Use `AtomicInteger/LongAdder` or a lock for compound actions. `volatile` is fine for a flag that one thread writes and others read.

questions.prompt: Complete the Java Memory Model happens-before rules.
questions.text: A write to a {1} field happens-before every later read of that field. An unlock of a monitor happens-before every later {2} of the same monitor. A call to Thread.{3}() happens-before every action in the started thread.
questions.explanation: These edges (plus thread join, final fields and executor submission) are what the `JMM` guarantees. Without an edge, one thread may never see another's write.

options.text: `true false 8 8 10`
options.why: Correct: first `CAS` 5 to 8 succeeds, second fails because the value is now 8, `getAndIncrement` returns 8 (value 9), `incrementAndGet` returns 10.

options.text: `true true 9 9 10`
options.why: The second `CAS` expects 5 but the value is 8, so it fails and returns false.

options.text: `true false 8 9 10 (getAndIncrement returns the new value)`
options.why: `getAndIncrement` returns the old value (8), not the new one (9).

options.text: `true false 8 8 9`
options.why: `incrementAndGet` increments 9 and returns 10, not 9.

questions.explanation: `compareAndSet(expect, update)` succeeds only if the current value equals expect, as one atomic hardware instruction. Retry loops around `CAS` give lock-free algorithms (and the ABA problem).

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: A Java `Callable<V>` can return a result and throw a checked exception, unlike `Runnable`.
questions.reason: `Runnable.run()` is declared to return `Object` and to throw `Exception`.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot be the correct explanation.
whys.b: R is false, so option b (both true) is wrong.
whys.c: Correct: Callable.call() returns V and may throw Exception. Runnable.run() returns void and declares no checked exceptions, so R is false.
whys.d: A is true, so option d (A false) is wrong.

questions.explanation: Executors accept both; `submit(Callable)` returns a `Future<V>` whose `get()` rethrows failures wrapped in `ExecutionException`.

questions.prompt: `Thread.sleep()`, like `Object.wait()`, releases every monitor the calling thread holds for the duration of the pause.

options.text: True
options.why: Wrong: this is true only for `wait()`; `sleep()` never gives up any monitor.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: `sleep()` holds on to its monitors, while `wait()` releases the one it was called on and reacquires it before returning.

questions.explanation: Only `Object.wait()` releases the monitor of the object it is called on; `Thread.sleep()` keeps all locks, so a sleeping thread inside `synchronized` blocks other threads that need the monitor.

options.text: `false false, flag cleared`
options.why: Correct: `sleep` sees the flag, throws `InterruptedException` and clears the flag, so both checks report false.

options.text: `true false, the flag is still set`
options.why: Wrong: the flag is cleared when `InterruptedException` is thrown, so `isInterrupted()` inside the catch is already false.

options.text: `true true, the flag is still set`
options.why: Wrong: `interrupted()` reads and clears the flag, and it was already cleared by the exception.

options.text: `false true, the flag is set again`
options.why: Wrong: nothing sets the flag again after the exception, so the later `interrupted()` call returns false.

questions.explanation: After catching `InterruptedException`, restore the status with `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()` unless you are really ending the thread. Verified by running it.

questions.prompt: A class has a `static synchronized` method and an instance `synchronized` method. Thread 1 is inside the static method; thread 2 calls the instance method on an object. What happens to thread 2?

options.text: It runs at once, since the two methods use different locks
options.why: Correct: `static synchronized` locks the `Class` object, instance synchronized locks `this`, so they do not exclude each other.

options.text: It blocks until thread 1 leaves, because both methods share the class monitor
options.why: Wrong: the instance method uses the object monitor, not the class monitor, so there is no contention.

options.text: It blocks only when both methods happen to have exactly the same name
options.why: Wrong: method names are irrelevant to locking; only the lock object matters.

options.text: It throws `IllegalMonitorStateException` because the lock kinds are mixed
options.why: Wrong: that exception comes from calling `wait` or `notify` without holding the monitor, not from mixing lock kinds.

questions.explanation: Guarding one piece of state with both kinds of method leaves it unprotected. Use one explicit lock object for the shared data.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Calling `unlock()` on a `ReentrantLock` from a thread that does not hold it throws `IllegalMonitorStateException`.
questions.reason: A `ReentrantLock` records its owning thread and a hold count, and only the owner may release it.

whys.a: Correct: the lock tracks its owner, which is exactly why a non-owner release is rejected (verified by running it).
whys.b: R is not an unrelated fact: the recorded owner is the direct reason for the exception.
whys.c: R is true: ReentrantLock keeps an owner and a hold count, so option c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true: the exception is thrown, so option d (A false) is wrong.

questions.explanation: A `Semaphore` has no owner, so any thread may release it. For a `ReentrantLock`, lock and unlock must pair up on the same thread, and unlock belongs in a `finally` block.
